newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Germany blocks deal on EMU budget pact.
newsitem.headline: Germany blocks deal on EMU budget pact.

text.p: German intransigence over the specifics of a budget pact for countries inside monetary union cast doubt on Monday over whether EU finance ministers could strike a deal by year-end.
The tough German stance left Europe's economic powerhouse virtually isolated, with only the Netherlands showing support for a budget stability pact that incorporates tougher conditions.
Juergen Stark, Germany's state secretary for finance, told journalists that "the timing is not decisive," and argued for an accord that was credible with financial markets and the public.

Enforcing budgetary rigour within economic and monetary union (EMU) is a prime concern for nearly all of the EU states, but nowhere is the objective greater than in Germany, a country wedded to sound monetary and budget policies.
Increasingly, German officials have become worried by what they perceive as a watering down of their initial proposal for the budget pact.
One of the main areas of concern is the lack of a precise definition of a severe economic downturn which would let governments running excessive deficits avoid sanctions.

Under a draft plan by the European Commission, a government found to have an annual deficit above three percent of total output would have to put forward a credible plan within a specified period -- 10 months -- to correct it.

If they failed, the offending country would have to make an initial deposit with the EU, worth 0.2 percent of gross domestic product (GDP). For every percentage point above the three percent threshold, an added fine of 0.1 percent of GDP would be levied.

But if a country could demonstrate that its poor finances were due to an extraordinary economic downturn, it could presumably avoid any penalty. The Commission did not quantify the magnitude of a recession, but Germany very much wants to.
"It is clear that one cannot define every exception, but we can reach a definition for a severe recession," Stark added.
Under a proposal from the EU's monetary committee, a numerical range, specifying the extent of an economic downturn, might be incorporated into a final budget agreement.

Yet because of wide differences in the budgetary and economic underpinnings of EU economies, any attempt at quantification would be offset by giving EU ministers discretion in evaulating the factors behind a country's recession.
In further attempt to bolster its bargaining position, Germany also argued that agreement on a post-EMU Exchange Rate Mechanism would have to coincide with a budget pact.
Diplomats said there were still some points to be negotiated over a new ERM that would link the single currency with those not participating in monetary union, expected in 1999.
In particular, this involved the bilateral exchange rate links between those countries outside EMU.
While Germany's tough stance cast a pall over Monday's ECOFIN Council, other EU diplomats offered an more optimistic assessment.
"It was a very constructive atmosphere," said one diplomat, adding that an accord could still be reached in time for the Dublin European Ciuncil on December 13 and 14.
